blocked.name: Sausage
blocking: Frankfurter note inverts the naming fact. It says 'Vienna answered with beef in the mix and called it a Wiener'. Vienna calls it a Frankfurter; it is Germany and everywhere else that calls the beef-and-pork version a Wiener — which is what makes the closing clause ('each city named its version after the other') true. As written the sentence contradicts itself. Fix to something like: 'Frankfurt made it from pork in a sheep casing; a Frankfurt butcher in Vienna put beef in the mix and still called it a Frankfurter, which is what Vienna calls it to this day — while Germany calls that version a Wiener.'

Mortadella row contradicts itself on the fat, and the chip is the wrong one. The grind cell says 'cubes of back fat folded back in'; the note says 'cubes of neck fat folded into the paste'. The Mortadella Bologna PGI specifies throat fat. Make both read throat fat (or neck fat, consistently) — one row cannot say two things about its own defining ingredient.

Rename 'Chorizo fresco'. In Spanish, chorizo fresco IS the fresh Spanish sausage — pimenton-led, grilled or fried, a real and distinct product. Using that name for the Mexican row reintroduces exactly the confusion 'On two chorizos with one name' exists to kill, and forces the note to open by denying its own title ('Not young Spanish chorizo'). Use 'Chorizo mexicano' (or 'Mexican chorizo', which is what the notes already call it in two places). Update the dish name only; facets and note stay as they are.

The 'By grind' nesting never reaches `state`, so it is not a second reading of the family — it is a flat list of chip labels. I ran the actual grow() from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts against this file: under 'coarse', grind chip 2 splits nine dishes into eight branches ('through a wide plate', 'fat left in visible pieces', 'hand-chopped', 'fat cut into cubes', 'lean and fat chopped separately', 'cut in chunks by hand', 'some of it ground finer to bind'), seven of them singletons, and `state` is drawn exactly once — for Cumberland and Boerewors, who pair only by accident of sharing 'chopped rather than minced'. Under 'fine' all four dishes fork into singletons and `state` is never drawn at all. The refinement guard cannot save it because it only fires when EVERY group is a singleton AND no dish has a chip 3. This is check 4: the lead chips (coarse/fine/emulsified) are shared, but chip 2 is not, and 'By grind' consumes chip 2 as a fork. Fix by normalising chip 2 into a shared move and pushing the idiosyncratic phrase to chip 3 or into the note. I verified this works: setting coarse chip 2 to 'hand-chopped' (Cumberland, Boerewors, Sai ua, Andouille, Lap cheong) vs 'through a plate' (Salsiccia, Longganisa, Chorizo, Kielbasa) produces coarse -> hand-chopped/through a plate -> sold raw / hung / cooked in the making, which is the reading the nesting promises. For 'fine', note that three of the four chip 2s are not grind at all but outcomes ('crumbles when it cooks', 'worked until it turns sticky', 'worked to a paste') — move those to the notes and either leave the cell at ['fine'] or give it a genuinely shared second chip, and state gets drawn there too.

The standfirst's third decision describes the wrong branch. 'chop it with ice until it sets like a custard under heat' is the emulsion — Frankfurter and Mortadella, 2 of the 5 dishes in the 'cooked in the making' branch. Andouille (smoked through), Kielbasa (scalded) and Boudin noir (poached) are cooked in the making and never see an ice-chopped paste. As written the standfirst collapses a `state` fork into a `grind` fork and misdescribes three rows. Rewrite the third option as the state decision — cook it in the making, by smoke, scald, steam or poach, so it is sold ready — and let 'On the emulsion' carry the ice-and-custard point, which it already does well.

Longganisa is two dishes written as one row. The spice cell hedges with 'sugar in the hamonado camp', and the state chip 'left to sour for a day or two' applies to de recado / Vigan but not to the sugared hamonado, whose note-line ('sugared until it caramelises in the pan') describes a different sausage. The note itself says Filipino cooks 'split it in two'. A conditional chip hides a fork the family's own rules say should be visible. Either split into two rows — 'Longganisa de recado' (garlic, cane vinegar, hung to sour) and 'Longganisa hamonado' (sugar, no souring, sold raw) — or drop 'sugar in the hamonado camp' and 'left to sour for a day or two' from the facets and let the note carry the split. Splitting is the better answer; it also gives the Philippines the same treatment Spain and Mexico get.
reasons: File under review: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/sausage.json (16 dishes, 5 facets, 3 nestings, 6 notes).

Check 1 PASSES: no two dishes share an identical row. Every pair differs in at least one chip; the closest pair (Salsiccia / Cumberland) shares state, smoke and the grind lead chip but separates on grind chip 2, spice and region.

Check 2 mostly passes. `state` (7/4/5), `grind` (9/4/2/1) and `region` (14 values) all fork. `smoke` is thin — 12 of 16 are 'no smoke' — but it earns its seat by doing the only work that separates Chorizo from 'Nduja and Kielbasa from Frankfurter. `spice` never appears in any nesting; that is deliberate and the standfirst says so ('a region answering the same question'), and its lead chips are too scattered (9 values over 16 dishes) to fork usefully. No column is pure decoration.

Check 3 near-passes. Two chips join things with 'and' — Lap cheong's 'sun and wind instead' and 'lean and fat chopped separately' — but each names one move rather than two, and both sit in refinement position where the tree does not fork on them. Not a problem. The real compound is a different kind: Longganisa's 'sugar in the hamonado camp' (see blocking).

Check 5 PASSES: `parent` is absent throughout, and 'On depth' argues the case explicitly and correctly. Chorizo fresco is not Spanish chorizo plus modifications (it is minus the drying and minus the pimenton), so it fails the IS-parent-plus test and should stay a sibling. Droewors and the Wiener are correctly left outside the table rather than hung under rows as fake children.

Check 6 PASSES: 14 regions over six continents — Maghreb, South Africa, Mexico, Philippines, Thailand, Turkey, China alongside the European rows. Not one continent wearing a global label. Two soft imbalances worth knowing but not blocking: Italy holds 3 of 16 seats while all of Latin America holds 1, and there is no salami anywhere in the table even though the 'Nduja note describes it as 'a cured salame that never firms up' — the reader is pointed at a thing that is not on the shelf. A salame row would also give the thin `smoke` column more work.

Check 7, minor items I would fix but am not blocking on: the dish is spelled 'Sai ua' while its own source is labelled 'Sai oua'; 'Lanna north' reads awkwardly as a region chip next to 'Guangdong' and 'Bologna' (the parallel form is 'Lanna' or 'northern Thailand'); the dish name is "'Nduja" but the notes drop the apostrophe three times ('nduja is spread on bread', 'And nduja, andouille'); Lap cheong's 'rose wine' will read as rose to most English speakers when mei kwei lu is a rose-scented baijiu; and 'Salsiccia' is the generic Italian word for sausage while the fennel-and-pepper row is really the Tuscan/central one — the same precision the chorizo note insists on.

Everything else in check 7 held up: the boerewors regulation (90% meat, 30% fat cap, no mechanically recovered meat), the Cumberland PGI and its coil, pimenton de la Vera dried over oak with Asturias as the smoking exception, sucuk's fenugreek and its cold-pan rendering, andouille over pecan against French tripe andouille, kielbasa's fine-ground paste gluing the coarse chunks, the inductilia etymology, and the blood-starch note (Burgos rice / sundae glass noodles / oatmeal / buckwheat / Blutwurst with neither).

Check 8 half-passes. The standfirst is specific and falsifiable rather than praising — 'Fresh chorizo and dry chorizo are not one sausage at two ages' is a real claim the table then backs. But its third branch is wrong about the table (see blocking).

blocked.name: Fresh cheese
blocking: Cottage cheese region: replace the chip 'England · United States'. ' · ' is the renderer's own chip separator — joinCell in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts joins chips with exactly that string — so this reads as two chips in the table but forks as a single node labelled 'England · United States' under 'By region'. I scanned all 18 families: this is the only chip in the entire corpus containing a middot. The corpus already carries 'England' and 'United States' as separate region values, so pick one lead country (the dressed-curd form and the name are American) and let the note carry the English farmhouse ancestry.

Standfirst: 'Every one of these is milk that has been made to quit, and eaten before it has time to ripen' is falsified by a dish in its own table. Feta spends months in the barrel and its note says outright that this 'is ripening rather than draining'; halloumi is 'brined for keeps' and dried mizithra 'stops being fresh'. Either soften the universal (e.g. '...and meant to be eaten young — feta, at two months in brine, is the one walking off the shelf') or drop the ripening clause and let the four decisions carry the sentence.

Wara's `set` cell is classified on a different basis from every other row and contradicts your own note. It leads 'plant sap' (classified by source) while Rubing's vine juice leads 'a food acid' (classified by mechanism) — yet note 1 says the Sodom apple sap 'is rennet by another name — a plant protease cutting casein at the same bond'. The rendered tree therefore strands Wara as a one-dish fifth branch, separated from the rennet cheeses it mechanically belongs with. Fix: set Wara's cell to ['rennet', 'from crushed Sodom apple leaves, not a calf', 'milk brought to a simmer']. That makes the tree agree with the note, retires the singleton branch, and leaves the `set` vocabulary as exactly the three routes the standfirst promises: acid (food acid, its own souring), enzyme (rennet), heat (whey reheated).

The `heat` cells break the 'By whether it melts' reading. Chips 2 and 3 for the eleven 'holds its shape' dishes are dish-unique colour ('browns in the pan', 'poached in sugar syrup', 'sets firm when baked with egg', 'grated over hot pasta', 'softens without running'...), and because canon.ts walks chips positionally it forks on them and shatters the group into eleven leaves before `curd` is reached. The reading renders at depth 2 using 1 of 3 facets. Fix: keep only the shared verdict in `heat` (chip 0) and move the per-dish colour into `note`. I simulated it against the real grow(): trimming `heat` alone takes the reading to depth 3 and forks 'holds its shape' into pressed under a weight / never pressed / pressed lightly. Trimming the colour off `curd` as well takes it to depth 4 on all three facets and lands Paneer and Rubing together under 'none at all', which is the true twin the family keeps pointing at.
Rubing: 'năiténg' uses ă (a-breve, U+0103) where pinyin third tone needs ǎ (a-caron, U+01CE). Correct to 'nǎiténg' in both the `set` chip and the note.

Queso Oaxaca note: 'Mozzarella's method arrived with Spanish dairying and was finished differently' asserts a transmission story that the dominant published account does not support — quesillo is generally dated to an accidental invention at Reyes Etla in 1885, centuries after Spanish cattle arrived, and the pasta filata link is usually credited to Italian/Dominican influence rather than Spanish dairying generally. It also cuts against your own note 4 ('Queso Oaxaca is not a Mexican mozzarella') and against the convergence framing you give Queijo coalho ('people who had never met it'). Either reword to the convergent reading, or name the specific transmission you believe and source it.
reasons: Check 1 (no duplicate rows) PASSES. I compared all 16 rows across all five facets: no two are identical. The closest pair is Ricotta and Mizithra, which share every lead chip (whey reheated / never pressed / barely any / holds its shape) and separate only on region and on their second and third chips — but they do separate, and note 4 defends the choice to keep them siblings rather than nesting one under the other. Paneer and Rubing are the same near-miss on the acid side and are likewise genuinely distinct rows.

Check 2 (dead dimensions) PASSES on the letter, with one caveat. No facet has the same value for every dish: set has 5 lead values, curd 4, salt 6, heat 3, region 11. The caveat is that salt never forks anything in any of the three readings (it sits third in nesting 1, which the tree never reaches, and is absent from the other two), and under nesting 1 the derived keyChips highlights 47 chips in `set` and zero in curd, salt, heat and region. I checked the whole corpus before flagging this and it is a house pattern, not a fresh-cheese fault (noodle-soup and skewer are 4/5 dead too), so I am not blocking on it — but nesting 2 rewritten as [heat, curd, salt] would put the standfirst's fourth decision to work at no cost.

Check 3 (compound chips) FAILS in one place: 'England · United States' in Cottage cheese's region. See blocking. The other joins I checked are fine — 'lemon juice or vinegar' is one decision with two interchangeable agents, 'sheep and goat milk' is one blend, 'north India and Pakistan' and 'Nigeria and Benin' are sub-region detail sitting below a lead chip that forks cleanly.

Check 4 (lead chip is the shared move) FAILS for the `heat` column. Every lead chip is correctly shared vocabulary, but in the eleven 'holds its shape' dishes the SECOND chip is dish-unique colour, and canon.ts consumes chips positionally: it forks on heat chip 0, then heat chip 1 shatters all eleven into singletons before `curd` is ever consulted. 'By whether it melts' therefore renders at depth 2 using 1 of its 3 declared facets — the flattest content reading in the corpus (braise 6/3-of-3, flatbread 6/3-of-3, frozen-dessert 6/3-of-3). See blocking for the demonstrated fix.

Check 5 (parent) PASSES, and is the strongest thing here. Burrata is the only `parent`, and it is the only dish that genuinely is another dish plus something. Chhena is correctly a sibling of Paneer rather than a child (it is not paneer-plus, it is the same curd forked earlier), Queso Oaxaca is correctly not hung under Mozzarella, and Mizithra is correctly not hung under Ricotta. Note 4 states the rule and the data obeys it.

Check 6 (parochial coverage) PASSES clearly. 16 dishes across 11 regions and 5 continents: South Asia 2, Italy 3, Greece 2, Mexico 2, Cyprus, Levant, Brazil, Finland, West Africa, China, and the England/US entry. Europe holds 7 of 16, which is heavy but not a global label on a European table — the Yunnan, West African and Brazilian entries are load-bearing rather than decorative, and each carries real mechanism.

Check 7 (facts) mostly PASSES. I checked and believe correct: mozzare = to cut off; the pH 5.2 stretching window; ricotta's albumin recovering at ~85C; casein's isoelectric point at 4.6 for labneh; halloumi's no-starter/cooked-in-whey pair; feta at up to a third goat; coalho meaning rennet in Portuguese; leipajuusto from cow colostrum in Ostrobothnia and Lapland; Calotropis procera as a casein-cutting protease, Fulani-made, wagashi in Benin and warankasi in Nigeria; burrata invented in Andria. Three problems are in blocking (the pinyin diacritic, the Oaxaca transmission claim, and the wara classification).

Check 8 (standfirst) FAILS on one clause. The three-routes-then-four-decisions structure is exactly right — specific, mechanical, no praise — but 'eaten before it has time to ripen' is contradicted inside its own table by Feta, whose note concedes that two months in brine 'is ripening rather than draining'. See blocking.

One more worth fixing but not blocking: Mizithra's salt cell reads ['barely any', 'salted hard only if it is to be dried']. That is a conditional in a fork column, and the condition describes a cheese that has left the family (dried mizithra is a grating cheese and not fresh). The note already says this in full, so the chip can simply go.
